newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian Renault workers throw car at embassy.
newsitem.headline: Belgian Renault workers throw car at embassy.

text.p: Belgian Renault workers, angered by the French carmaker's decision to close their plant, hurled a car chassis across police barricades on Friday as they demonstrated outside the French embassy.

Chanting "Renault Stays Open", the men picked up a yellow Renault Megane, brought from their assembly plant in Vilvoorde near Brussels, and threw it at the embassy, barely missing policemen and fellow protestors.

The noisy demonstration by at least 500 workers marked the start of a day of action by unions seeking a reversal of the closure, scheduled for July, to protect the plant's 3,100 jobs and employment at Belgian suppliers.

Demonstrators, who travelled from Vilvoorde in a fleet of 10 buses, blew whistles and horns and threw firecrackers at the embassy where the shutters were down on the windows of the first two floors. A small delegation met the French ambassador.
A union spokesman complained the ambassador showed little understanding.
"He is a typical French ambassador, he is more concerned about a wreck landing in his front garden than the loss of 3,100 jobs," he said.
The French state holds a 46 percent stake in Renault and unions have charged that Renault targeted the Belgian plant in its reorganisation drive to prevent heavy job losses in France.

The demonstrators were due to visit the assembly plants of other carmakers later on Friday, where workers are expected to down tools for one hour per shift to show their sympathy for their Renault colleagues.
The Volkswagen plant in Vorst led the way with the morning shift striking between nine and 10 a.m. (0800 and 0900 GMT). Stoppages were also planned at Opel, Volvo and Ford plants.
Joining in the protest, Renault dealers around the country closed their doors for all or part of the day.
"We want to show our dissatifaction with the decision by Renault management," a spokesman for the association of Renault dealers said.

But any protest would be mainly symbolic. "We must be cautious, there are 4,000 families which depend on Renault -- dealers, agents, mechanics, there are at least 400,000 Renault owners -- we can't leave those people out in the cold," he said.

There were cautious words too from the associations of carmakers, car importers, suppliers, dealers, and repairers, which in a joint statement warned against an all-out boycott which could cost thousands of jobs.
The sector employs 11.8 percent of Belgium's working population.

The associations blamed overcapacity, flagging demand and "murderous competition" for Renault's decision to close the plant, but also pointed the finger at the Belgian government which had created "a negative fiscal climate" for car owners.
The associations' joint Brussels building was decked in black flags out of sympathy with the sacked Renault workers.
